title: Free while living
hook: liberation is possible in this life, not only after

segments.voice: Yesterday, the long round of births, and Guru Arjan's line: this human body is your turn. Your line was this life is the chance. What did you do before the evening came? Day one thousand three hundred sixty-nine.

Liberation sounds like something that happens at the end. A gate at the far side of a long road. A reward after the last breath. It's easy to picture it that way, and yesterday's lesson could be heard like that: this life is the turn, so the prize must come after. But Sikh scripture has a phrase that turns that picture inside out. Two words, jivan mukat. Free while living. Not free someday. Free while you still have a job, a family, a phone that won't stop buzzing. Today asks what that freedom could possibly look like on a weekday.
screen: `A GATE AT THE END OF THE ROAD?` → `JIVAN MUKAT.` → `FREE WHILE YOU STILL HAVE A JOB.`

segments.voice: Start with the phrase. Jivan means life, living. Mukat means freed, released. Put together: one who is liberated while alive. The Granth uses it of people walking around in the world, not only of souls after death. In Guru Arjan's Sukhmani Sahib there's a passage that says, in paraphrase: the one who takes the Lord's will to heart is called free while living. To that person, joy and sorrow are alike. There is lasting bliss, and no separation. Notice what's missing. It doesn't say the free person has no sorrow. It says sorrow and joy weigh the same. The storms still come. They just don't knock the person off the ground. Freedom from what? Not from the world. Sikh life stays in the world: family, work, langar, sangat. The freedom is from being pushed around inside: by ego, by fear, by the endless wanting more. It connects to the week's thread. Order and effort: you work, and accept the hukam. Deeds and grace: you do good and leave the door to the One. A person who can actually live like that, here, is what jivan mukat names. That matters on an ordinary day. If freedom were only after death, there'd be nothing to taste now. Jivan mukat says the taste is available in this life, even in a hard week, even for a moment at a time. Free now.
screen: `JIVAN MUKAT: FREED WHILE ALIVE.` · `JOY AND SORROW, ALIKE.` · `FREE INSIDE, NOT FROM THE WORLD.` · `A TASTE, NOW, IN THIS LIFE.` · then, large: `FREE NOW.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: live freely today. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind one good thing from this week, and let it sit in front of you. Then bring one hard thing, and set it beside the good one. Don't push the hard one away or hold on to the good one. Just let them sit side by side, the same weight, while you keep breathing. If you pray, you can hold both as within the will. If you don't, just notice the breath going on underneath both. The bell holds the time.
Free while living. Jivan mukat: liberated in this life, not only after it, where joy and sorrow weigh the same. Today's word.

Your line: free now. Today, when something goes wrong, take one breath before you react, and see if you can meet it with the same steadiness as something going right. Day one thousand three hundred sixty-nine.

howItsDone: Sikhs recite Sukhmani Sahib, which describes the one who takes the Lord's will to heart as free while living, and Sikh teaching places that freedom inside family life, work and service, not apart from them.

trapdoor: what you thought: liberation is a reward that comes after you die.
what it means: jivan mukat, freed while living, steady in joy and sorrow.
what a scholar hears: Sukhmani names the one who takes the Lord's will to heart as free while living, in the middle of ordinary life.

notes: Paraphrase of 'prabh kee aagiaa aatam hitaavai, jeevan mukat sou kahaavai; taisaa harakh taisaa us sog, sadaa anand tah nahee biog' (Sukhmani, Ang 275); please confirm the Ang and that these lines belong to the same passage.
The glosses jivan = life and mukat = freed are plain glosses, not an argued etymology; please confirm.
